newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mobutu to return home in last chance attempt.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to return home in last chance attempt.

text.p: Ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko planned to return home from France on Friday for a last-ditch attempt to save his crumbling authority.

A spokesman said the Zairean leader, who has spent most of his time in Europe since an operation for prostate cancer in August, would leave Nice airport at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) and would arrive in Kinshasa at 3 p.m.(1400 GMT).

Mobutu issued an appeal late on Thursday for a ceasefire in Zaire, where rebel forces have won control of about a fifth of the country, and the creation of a national council to find a solution to the crisis.
The statement, in which he called on Zaireans "to rise together," came as France called on its nationals to leave Zaire and positioned its troops to help to evacuate them from Kinshasa if necessary.
The United States said it too was making contingency plans to pull out Americans.

Mobutu, who has held power for more than 30 years, has been threatened before by armed opponents but rebels have never made such deep advances and his notoriously ill-disciplined army has rarely performed as poorly.
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga, has said his father did not rule out talks with the rebels led by Laurent Kabila but this had to be done in agreement with the government and parliament.
The rebels, who control such major cities as Kisangani and Goma, insist that only face-to-face talks between Kabila and Mobutu can halt the fighting.

"I call on those who hold any responsibilities and who love their country to gather together to resolve the crisis," Mobutu said in a written statement sent to news agencies in Paris from his villa on the French Riviera.

He said he welcomed all regional and international efforts to bring peace, adding: "There must be a ceasefire to put an end to the sufferings which our people are enduring and to allow humanitarian aid to be sent in safe conditions to those who need it."
He also said a campaign to organise new elections should begin without delay "to designate representatives freely chosen by the people."
